title: From food to tech to travel: the best student deals and discounts
summary:
You can save money at university, especially using schemes such as UNiDAYS, Student Beans or TOTUM

  • ‘Watch your spending, use free perks’: an insider’s tips on student money

With rents on the up and food costing more, maintenance loans are stretched thinner than ever. Knowing how, and where, to get a discount can make a real difference.

A golden rule is to register with the big discount websites and apps – UNiDAYS, Student Beans and TOTUM – using your university email address as soon as you have one. Each has a slightly different roster of retailers, so it is worth signing up to all three.

full_text:
With rents on the up and food costing more, maintenance loans are stretched thinner than ever. Knowing how, and where, to get a discount can make a real difference.

A golden rule is to register with the big discount websites and apps – UNiDAYS, Student Beans and TOTUM – using your university email address as soon as you have one. Each has a slightly different roster of retailers, so it is worth signing up to all three.

Many of the deals below are only unlocked once you have verified your student status. The sites explain how to do this. If you are unable to verify using email, you may be able to upload, for example, an acceptance letter from your university.

Food and essentials

Boots: an Advantage Card gets you 10% off thousands of products instore and online – handy for weekly toiletries and the odd emergency paracetamol run. You need to apply for a card then go into a shop with a valid student ID to activate your membership and qualify for the discounts.

Marks & Spencer: 25% off in store’s “food on the move” range through UNiDAYS. This range includes sandwiches, wraps, poké bowls and salads, plus a variety of snacks.

Uber One: after a four-week free trial, students get half-price membership (£2.49 a month), for discounted delivery and takeaways – useful on the days when a big supermarket shop feels like one task too many.

The Co-op: 10% off your shop in-store – but now only for some students, such as those with a Young Scot card. Central Co-op and Southern Co-op give Student Beans members 10% off at their participating stores.

Going out

Many pub and restaurant chains – including Greene King, Pizza Express and Zizzi – offer money off. Greene King offers 20% off all food and drinks (show your student ID at the bar to get one of its 20% off student cards).

Tech and subscriptions

Amazon Prime for Students: new sign-ups get six months of Prime free, after which it drops to half price (£4.49 a month).

Link your Amazon and Deliveroo accounts through a site such as UNiDAYS and you will also get a year’s worth of Deliveroo Plus – which gets you free delivery on orders above £15 from restaurants, or above £25 from shops – at no extra cost instead of the usual £3.49 a month.

Kindle Unlimited: claim 30 days free through UNiDAYS – useful for clearing a reading list without buying every set text.

Microsoft 365: many universities give students free access to the full Office suite – Word, Excel, PowerPoint and Outlook – via their institution’s IT department, so check before you pay for anything.

Spotify Premium: one month free, then £5.99 a month – roughly half the standard price.

Apple: offers “education pricing” – a variety of reductions on MacBooks and other items – to students who have a UNiDAYS account.

Microsoft: up to 15% off items such as laptops and accessories bought directly.

Adobe Creative Cloud: If you are on a creative course or just want to develop your skills, Adobe offers a 75% saving on its Pro subscription for students, reducing the cost from £66.49 a month to £16.24.

Gyms and fitness

The Gym Group: up to 25% off via the student discount sites.

Fitness First: up to 25% off via the student discount sites.

Strava: 30 days of its premium plan for free, then 50% off the subscription (taking it down to £27.49 a year).

University gyms are almost always cheaper than commercial ones, and BUCS (British Universities and Colleges Sport) UNIversal Gym scheme means if your own university’s gym is signed up, you can use any other participating gym for free. That’s great if you are visiting friends or family at or near another campus and don’t want to break your routine.

Travel

FlixBus: 20% off fares via UNiDAYS and Student Beans.

National Express: up to 20% off coach tickets via UNiDAYS, Student Beans and TOTUM.

16-25 Railcard: one-third off most rail fares (you can get one for free for four years if you open a Santander Edge student current account). Alternatively, students get 15% off the cost of the card via Student Beans and UNiDAYS – typically it’s £35 a year.

Fashion

Asos and Nike offer 10% off via UNiDAYS, Student Beans and TOTUM, with JD Sports offering 20%.

Urban Outfitters has 10% off all year-round for students.

Always carry proof of student status – a university ID card, or a UNiDAYS, Student Beans or TOTUM card or login.

Also, don’t be afraid to ask if a student discount isn’t advertised. Many independent shops and cafes offer one but don’t always put up a sign.

title: ‘Watch your spending, use free perks’: an insider’s tips on student money
summary:
Avoid getting into debt at university with tricks to save cash, earn extra funds and have a good time

  • The best student deals and discounts

Over the past two years university student Erin has been giving Martin Lewis a run for his money when it comes to hunting down the best hacks, tips and tricks to save cash and earn money.

The 21-year-old has seen Oasis for free; earned tickets to race days; made money from selling secondhand clothes (£200 in one weekend alone); and enjoyed cut-price treats with friends.

full_text:
Over the past two years university student Erin has been giving Martin Lewis a run for his money when it comes to hunting down the best hacks, tips and tricks to save cash and earn money.

The 21-year-old has seen Oasis for free; earned tickets to race days; made money from selling secondhand clothes (£200 in one weekend alone); and enjoyed cut-price treats with friends.

On Thursday, tens of thousands of young people found out if they had achieved the grades for the course of their choice. Now, as they celebrate, or hurriedly activate, their plan B, the day-to-day costs of student life probably aren’t uppermost in their mind. But perhaps they should be: research from Nationwide Building Society reveals that money mistakes dominate students’ list of regrets.

From failing to budget and track spending properly, overspending on nights out and relying too heavily on their overdraft, to blowing their entire student loan payment in the first few weeks, six of the top seven mistakes students have made are related to money.

“Our research shows just how much more financial pressure today’s students feel compared with previous generations,” says Tom Riley, Nationwide’s director of retail products.

Erin, who is about to start the third year of a psychology and cognitive neuroscience degree at the University of Nottingham, says going to university has “taught me loads” about managing money.

“Before I started, I’d worked and saved, but when that student loan lands in your account, it can feel a bit like free money,” she says. “It’s easy to fall into ‘girl math’ logic and justify little extras that quickly add up.”

She says that working before university and during the holidays “definitely gave me a better sense of what things actually cost”.

Erin sets herself a budget and has a rule that if she needs to go over it, she has to dip into the savings earned from her job, which, she says, focuses the mind on whether she needs to spend that money.

Her view is that wherever possible, the money she is saving “is not money I can spend [as] that is undoing all the good work I’ve done”.

To cut spending, she makes the most of discounts and deals, and joins with friends to maximise the benefits. She, and some of her friends, have Nationwide FlexStudent bank accounts, which offers a £10 Just Eat voucher every month for the first 12 months.

In her first year, she says, they pooled their vouchers and had “floor picnics” in their halls of residence, where they would all sit and share their takeaways.

It was, she says, “a life-saver because we didn’t have great cooking facilities and were on really limited budgets … It was a nice way to treat ourselves”.

Saving money has not meant missing out on a social life, as she has found ways to get into gigs and events that do not involve spending.

As a brand rep for a company that organises days out at racecourses around the UK, she gets a free ticket and transport to any events she has promoted. Tickets can be pricey for these “race day” outings, which are popular with students. She had to post a promotional message on her social media and send a link to three group chats, and she earned commission on any ticket bought via her link.

Signing up with an agency for voluntary work at events has also got her into gigs and festivals for nothing. “I got to see Oasis last year for free,” she says. “I think I did an eight-hour shift scanning tickets.” Her shift finished just as the support act ended, so she was able to watch the band’s entire set. “I was front row – that would have cost a lot of money,” she says. Her stint included a staff meal voucher.

Last year, she volunteered at Truck festival in Oxfordshire. Typically, she says, with volunteering at a festival, you may have to do two or three shifts over the weekend, but still get plenty of free time to enjoy the event.

Her savings pay for things she cannot get for free: this year the big thing she was saving for was the college ski trip. “Every bit I saved I put towards that.”

Here are her money-saving tips:

Think in hours, not pounds Before buying something, work out how many hours you would need to work to pay for it. “A couple of cocktails on a night out can easily be the equivalent of more than an hour’s wages from a summer job. It’s a good reality check and makes me think twice about the impulse purchases.”

Volunteer for freebies and perks There are lots of firms that recruit volunteers for festivals and one-day events – Erin signed up with Festaff and Wicked Events.

Turn fashion into a side hustle Erin snaps up quality pieces from charity shops and similar, some of which she upcycles before selling them on platforms such as Vinted, along with her own items that she no longer wants.

Look out for opportunities A lot of universities have brand ambassador programmes. Students often act as brand reps for nightclubs, as well as other events and venues.

Pool rewards with friends You could combine discounts and deals with housemates or friends to get better value and reduce everyday spending.

title: Science or fiction? Shadowy ‘paper mills’ let you pay to be a published author – of fraudulent research
summary:
Paper mill activity has exploded in recent years, polluting the scientific ecosystem with falsified data and compromising medical research

Dr Reese Richardson’s phone constantly buzzes with notifications. The scientific research integrity specialist has been tracking shadowy organisations known as “paper mills”, which turn a profit by offering fraudulent academic authorship of scientific papers, IP registrations and other scholarly outputs.

For a fee, paper mills offer to list people as authors of scientific journal articles, often of falsified research that bypasses the peer review process.

full_text:
Dr Reese Richardson’s phone constantly buzzes with notifications. The scientific research integrity specialist has been tracking shadowy organisations known as “paper mills”, which turn a profit by offering fraudulent academic authorship of scientific papers, IP registrations and other scholarly outputs.

For a fee, paper mills offer to list people as authors of scientific journal articles, often of falsified research that bypasses the peer review process.

Richardson has joined dozens of groups across apps such as Telegram, WhatsApp and Facebook where a buffet of fraudulent and fabricated research is advertised to hundreds of members. “I can just look through my notifications and I can see that I’ve gotten, like, 20 WhatsApp messages from paper mills in the last 24 hours,” he says.

Scientists are under constant pressure to publish new research papers which, in many parts of the world, remain the currency of academia. They beget more grant funding and accolades, and enhance academic profiles. But robust, high-quality science takes time, and papers can take years to get published.

Paper mills offer a fraudulent shortcut, using instant messaging and social media platforms to find prospective buyers looking for papers and patents to stack their CVs. According to an analysis Richardson conducted with Anna Abalkina and Spencer Hong, the median price to buy authorship is around US$800 (A$1,150).

In a recent paper, which has not yet been peer reviewed, the trio of scientists led by Richardson, formerly at Northwestern University in the US, detailed more than 18,000 advertisements from seven paper mills across seven countries between 2020 and 2026.

“We wanted to get an idea, across a wide range of paper mills, countries, topics and product types how much these things actually go for,” he says. “What we put together is the largest ever dataset of paper mill advertisements.”

They found many groups advertising authorship of scientific manuscripts across Telegram, Facebook and various websites for as little as US$30.

In the last 15 years, paper mill activity has exploded, with one estimate produced by Richardson in 2025 suggesting their products have been doubling approximately every 18 months. The journal articles produced by these paper mills typically bypass the accepted scientific editorial process of peer review, either because the journals do not institute those processes or because editors are themselves part of paper mill activities.

Sign up for a weekly email featuring our best reads

This amounts to an industrialised injection of falsified data, polluting the scientific ecosystem and compromising medical research, drug discovery and clinical trials. The scale is massive: in 2023, Hindawi, a now defunct journal brand owned by major publisher Wiley, retracted more than 8,000 articles. A further 3,000 retractions came by the end of 2024.

Richardson says his research is a useful starting point for trying to grapple with how and where paper mills operate, and who they target. The advertisements are like fingerprints at a crime scene, potential evidence of malicious activity. “You can get a lot of information from the advertisements,” he says. He has directly tracked some of these to fraudulent papers in the scientific literature.

Designs and IP for sale

Other advertisements relate to copyrights and design registrations, another area ripe for fraud, which may provide buyers with legitimate intellectual property rights. Richardson notes one of the reasons to do this is to bolster resumes in service of academic advancement.

Richardson has previously identified exploitation of IP systems in the UK, finding thousands of design registrations. His new work identifies 12 instances where design registrations were advertised by a paper mill operating in India and catering to Indian academics.

Richardson’s data shows these design registrations are being advertised as “Australian design patents”. The paper mills sell positions as “owners” of design registrations, charging between $95 and $150 per owner, for up to eight people to be registered on any given design. A design registration application through IP Australia costs $200 in total.

Guardian Australia identified cases where the registrations were listed as patents on CVs.

“They’re using the services of the Australian government to defraud others,” Richardson says. He points to several unusual instances of design registrations.

One Australian design registration, for an “AI based membrane bioreactor for treatment of wastewater”, belongs to six people whom Guardian Australia has traced to research institutes in India. Five of the six were contacted; none responded to requests for comment.

A “GS Collison” is listed under the address for service on the registration, as well as for 11 other design registrations. However, there is no trace online of GS Collison as an entity, and the address listed for it – level 11 in one of Sydney’s Darling Park towers – corresponds to the offices of IAG, an insurance firm. In response to questions from Guardian Australia, an IAG spokesperson noted level 11 is occupied by a series of meeting rooms.

Another example, a “Smart humanoid robot for industrial applications”, includes Dr Nilesh Torwane, a postdoctoral researcher at the University of Queensland as a design owner. When contacted by Guardian Australia, Torwane says he “did no design work on the product” but was invited to be named on the design by others listed on the registration. He also noted the registration “never formed part of any claim I have made for professional or academic advancement”.

“I have disclosed the matter proactively to the University and am taking steps to correct the record, including seeking removal of my name from the registration,” Torwane says. Guardian Australia is not suggesting that the registration is not for a legitimate product, only that Torwane was not involved in its design.

When contacted by Guardian Australia, a spokesperson for IP Australia suggested it was not aware of the research paper by Richardson and colleagues.

“IP Australia welcomes any information that may indicate that the designs registration system is not being used for its intended purposes, and we will consider the implications raised by the research paper. However, we have no data to suggest that there is widespread misuse of the Australian designs registration system in the manner suggested.”

Though Richardson’s paper goes some way to exploring how paper mills are operating, the mills remain “shadowy organisations”, according to Prof Adrian Barnett, a metascience researcher at the Queensland University of Technology who has previously published with Richardson.

“It could be some techie kid in their bedroom, or some of them might be larger organisations that even have morning teas and employees of the month,” he says. “Who knows? But we can see they’re making a decent amount of money.”

While Richardson is being interviewed, his phone buzzes again: another advertisement in a WhatsApp group. The organisations are operating at such a scale and speed it’s hard to keep up.

“We’ve still barely scratched the surface,” he says.

title: Devendra Nath Mahto | The making of an agitator
summary: The student leader has emerged as the most prominent face of the agitation over alleged irregularities in the conduct of exams in Jharkhand
full_text:
On August 10, as thousands of Jharkhand students marched in the capital, Ranchi, to gherao the State Assembly, Devendra Nath Mahto appeared amid the crowd, held aloft by his supporters, with a framed photograph of former Jharkhand Chief Minister Shibu Soren in one hand and the other raised towards the protesters. Flower petals were showered on him as cameras and mobile phones followed his movements.

For a man who has spent a decade organising student protests, the attention is new only in scale. Mr. Mahto, 33, has emerged as the most prominent face of the agitation over alleged irregularities in the 14th Jharkhand Public Service Commission (JPSC) preliminary and Jharkhand Staff Selection Commission (JSSC) examinations. He has been on an indefinite hunger strike since August 2, and was hospitalised after the August 10 march, entering the 15th day of his fast on Sunday (August 9, 2026).

The current agitation began days after the JPSC results were declared on July 2. A Jharkhand Loktantrik Krantikari Morcha (JLKM) leader, Mr. Mahto held a press conference on July 5, questioning the examination process, and submitted a set of demands to the Governor two days later. On July 8, protesters burnt an effigy of the JPSC chairman at Albert Ekka Chowk. After a meeting with Chief Minister Hemant Soren on July 20 yielded little, Mr. Mahto called for an indefinite sit-in at Bapu Vatika in Morabadi on July 25, later moving to Jaipal Singh Munda Stadium.

The protest has since grown, with gheraos, marches and a continued hunger strike of at least six other students, even after three rounds of talks with the government that yielded in cancellation of JPSC prelims and backlog exams of 2023-25. However, Mr. Mahto says the protest will not be called off until all exams conducted by the TDPL (a private exam conducting agency) are cancelled, including JSSC-CGL, and CBI investigation is recommended.

A stage of students

Owing to his political affiliations, a section of students, days into the protest, set up a different stage to keep their distance from “politics” and insisting that the stage remain independent of political parties. Mr. Mahto responded by refusing to take the stage again when politics became a point of discussion. His bed was moved below the stage, as he affirmed, “This is the stage of students and their issues, not of any political party.”

There was little in Mr. Mahto’s early life to suggest a political career. Son of Vishambar Mahto, a retired government teacher, he grew up in Rahe village in Ranchi district. His elder brother Dhaneshwar Mahto is a farmer. He was sent to Bundu, about 10 km from the village, for his matriculation and intermediate education. He later moved to Ranchi. He completed his B.Ed in Hazaribagh and postgraduate studies in Sanskrit and regional languages in Ranchi University till 2022.

“He wanted to be a teacher,” his brother said. “As any village child, he also wanted a simple government job to lead his life. That is why good education was prioritised.”

That changed in college. In 2016, Mr. Mahto began protesting over student scholarships. He subsequently became involved in demonstrations over recruitment rules, paper leaks and alleged irregularities in JPSC and JSSC exams. According to friends, he has led around a dozen agitations since 2015.

“He never spoke of becoming a political leader,” his brother said. “He spoke about raising his voice against injustice and for people’s rights. He says he does not care if anything happens to him.”

Friends describe him as an able orator, persistent and unusually tolerant. Chandan Kumar, a close friend and colleague from college since 2016, said Mahto could bring students together and lead their voices. Even though Chandan distances himself from politics, he supports Mr. Mahto for the student’s cause.

“He is always thinking about the welfare of Jharkhand’s students,” Mr. Kumar said. His political influences extend beyond the Mahtos. Friends say he began reading B.R. Ambedkar, Mahatma Gandhi and Martin Luther King Jr. in college and later developed an interest in Jharkhand leaders such as Nirmal Mahto and Vinod Bihari Mahto. He often quotes Vinod Bihari Mahto’s slogan, “Padho aur lado” — study and fight.

The protests also came at a personal cost. During his first major agitation against alleged irregularities in the sixth JPSC examination, his mother died of cancer in 2019. Since then, his visits to his house have become less frequent.

“Whatever work he picks he does it with utmost honesty and with dedication till he achieves the goal. His hard work inspires us so we support him,” his brother said, who had also appeared for competitive exams.

Turn to politics

Mr. Mahto has himself appeared for at least four JPSC preliminaries, JSSC-CGL and TGT examinations.

In 2022, he emerged alongside Jairam Mahto during protests over the inclusion of Bhojpuri, Magahi and Angika as regional languages in JSSC examinations. The following year, he became a prominent face of the agitation against the 60:40 employment policy, popularising the slogan “60-40 nay chalto”.

After protesters gheraoed the JSSC office in January 2024 over the alleged leakage of the JSSC-CGL examination paper, the examination was cancelled. But Mr. Mahto and other protesters were booked in a case that included charges related to rioting, unlawful assembly, attempt to murder and assault, according to Chandan.

“He transformed into a prominent chatra neta soon leading Jharkhand State Students’ Union, and after that it is hard to resist the mainstream politics,” a close associate said. “He wants to reach Parliament,” he said.

The JLKM, founded by activist-politician Jairam Mahto, became a political vehicle, with Devendra Nath Mahto increasingly involved in its activities. He contested the 2024 Lok Sabha election independently from Ranchi and finished third, securing more than 1.4 lakh votes and then the 2025 Vidhan Sabha election from his home constituency Silli on the JLKM ticket. He was arrested during the nomination period in 2024 election and filed his nomination from jail. He says the move into politics was a natural extension of his activism.

“Since 2015, we have been agitating and constantly raising our voice about JPSC, JSSC and other examination irregularities. During this time, there were BJP, JMM and Congress governments, but there was no solution to the students’ issues,” he said. “If the solution has to come from a political government, then why shouldn’t students themselves be part of that politics?”

The JLKM’s politics also includes the demand to extend Scheduled Tribe reservation to the Kudmi community, to which Mr. Mahto and Jairam Mahto belong. Yet, amid the current agitation, Mr. Mahto insists that his political identity must not eclipse the issue that brought him there.

“This is not my voice. This is the voice of lakhs of aspirants who have been affected, and their mothers who await a better future,” he said. “I knew this movement would grow bigger because this is a student movement.” For now, he says, he will remain on hunger strike. “The government has given us nothing in writing. How can I end my strike until the students are satisfied with the government’s response?” he asked.

title: heise-Angebot: Impact Labs: Workshopreihe für Frauen in IT-Berufen startet
summary: Zwei Online-Workshops im Oktober und Dezember behandeln das Auftreten in Tech-Teams und Verhandlungsführung – in Gruppen von höchstens 20 Personen.
full_text:
Inhaltsverzeichnis

Fachliche Exzellenz entscheidet selten allein über die nächste Rolle, das nächste Projekt oder das nächste Gehaltsband. Wer in Meetings gehört wird und den eigenen Beitrag präzise benennen kann, verschafft sich Handlungsspielraum – eine Kompetenz, die in technischen Ausbildungswegen kaum systematisch vermittelt wird. An dieser Lücke setzen die neuen Women in Tech Impact Labs an.

Weiterlesen nach der Anzeige

Arbeiten an eigenen Fällen

Das Format ist als praxisorientierter Workshop angelegt: In kleinen Gruppen arbeiten die Teilnehmerinnen an konkreten Fragestellungen aus dem eigenen Berufsalltag und entwickeln gemeinsam mit erfahrenen Expertinnen und Coaches Lösungen, die sich unmittelbar anwenden lassen. Im Fokus stehen Werkzeuge für souveränes Auftreten, wirksame Kommunikation und erfolgreiche Verhandlungen. Angesprochen sind Frauen aus Technologie, IT und Cybersecurity oder anderen männerdominierten Bereichen, die ihre berufliche Entwicklung aktiv gestalten möchten – von Nachwuchstalenten bis zu Führungskräften.

Zwei Termine, zwei Themen

9. Oktober 2026 – „Souverän in der Männerdomäne – Kommunikation & Präsenz“: Status-Spiele erkennen und steuern (High Talk/Low Talk), Raum einnehmen in Videokonferenzen, Techniken gegen Unterbrechungen. Ziel ist erhöhte Sichtbarkeit und mehr Standing in Meetings und bei Präsentationen.

4. Dezember 2026 – „Die Kunst der Verhandlung & strategische Selbstvermarktung“: Psychologie der Verhandlung im IT-Kontext, den eigenen Marktwert präzise definieren, Umgang mit Einwänden und „Killerphrasen“. Als Ergebnis nehmen die Teilnehmerinnen einen individuellen „Argumentations-Leitfaden“ für das nächste Personalgespräch mit.

Beide Impact Labs leitet Fenna zur Horst, zertifizierter Business Coach, Trainerin sowie Betriebs- und Kommunikationswirtin mit langjähriger Führungserfahrung in Konzern und Mittelstand. Gesponsert werden beide Termine von Huawei.

Die Workshops finden online über Zoom statt. Für einen intensiven Austausch ist die Gruppengröße auf höchstens 20 Personen begrenzt. Hinzu kommt der Austausch in der heise Women in Tech Community mit rund 900 Mitgliedern. Die Teilnahme lässt sich in vielen Unternehmen über das Weiterbildungsbudget abrechnen – eine Rücksprache mit der jeweiligen Führungskraft oder Personalabteilung klärt, ob der Arbeitgeber die Kosten übernimmt.

Weiterlesen nach der Anzeige
translated_text:
Table of Contents

Technical excellence rarely determines the next role, the next project or the next salary range. Anyone who is heard in meetings and can precisely state their own contribution gives themselves room for maneuver - a skill that is rarely taught systematically in technical training courses. The new Women in Tech Impact Labs address this gap.

Read more after the ad

Working on your own cases

The format is designed as a practice-oriented workshop: In small groups, the participants work on specific questions from their own everyday working life and, together with experienced experts and coaches, develop solutions that can be applied immediately. The focus is on tools for a confident appearance, effective communication and successful negotiations. Targeted are women from technology, IT and cybersecurity or other male-dominated areas who want to actively shape their professional development - from young talent to managers.

Two dates, two topics

October 9, 2026 - "Sovereign in the male domain - Communication & Presence": Recognizing and controlling status games (high talk/low talk), taking up space in video conferences, techniques against interruptions. The goal is increased visibility and more standing in meetings and presentations.

December 4, 2026 - “The art of negotiation & strategic self-marketing”: Psychology of negotiation in the IT context, precisely defining your own market value, dealing with objections and “killer phrases”. As a result, the participants take an individual “argumentation guide” with them for the next personnel interview.

Both Impact Labs are headed by Fenna zur Horst, a certified business coach, trainer and business and communications economist with many years of management experience in corporations and medium-sized companies. Both dates are sponsored by Huawei.

The workshops take place online via Zoom. For an intensive exchange, the group size is limited to a maximum of 20 people. There is also the exchange in the heise Women in Tech Community with around 900 members. In many companies, participation can be billed through the training budget - a consultation with the respective manager or human resources department will clarify whether the employer will cover the costs.

Read more after the ad
